screens.body:
Design validation asks one question: "does this design actually satisfy the requirements?" You check BEFORE coding, because a flaw caught in a diagram costs a conversation — the same flaw caught after release costs a rewrite.

Think of it like proofreading an essay before printing fifty copies. The checking IS the work; the printing is just mechanics.

options: Checking the design satisfies requirements, before coding
Testing the finished app with users
Writing more code to fix bugs
check.question: Design validation means…

screens.heading: Check before you build
screens.keyPoint: Validate on paper; it's the cheapest place to be wrong.

screens.body:
Traceability is the paper trail from requirement to design: every requirement should point to the design pieces that satisfy it, and every design piece should point back to a requirement it serves.

Two failure modes: orphans (a design piece with no requirement — why are we building this?) and gaps (a requirement with no design — whoops). A simple traceability table — requirements down the side, design pieces across the top — makes both visible instantly.

options: Every requirement links to design pieces and back — no orphans, no gaps
check.question: Traceability means…

screens.heading: The paper trail
screens.keyPoint: Every requirement accounted for; nothing extra.

screens.body:
A walkthrough is the team reading the design together, out loud, hunting for problems. The designer presents; everyone else plays detective with a checklist: Are all requirements covered? Are the data rules consistent? Can this actually be built?

Checklists matter because brains skip things. "Did we define valid values for every field?" is boring to ask and expensive to forget. Reviews feel slow — they're the fastest way to avoid building the wrong system.

options: The team reviews the design together using a checklist
check.question: A design walkthrough is…

screens.heading: Fresh eyes find flaws

screens.body:
Some things change over time — and state machine diagrams model exactly that. An object sits in a STATE (a task is "open"), an EVENT happens ("someone accepts it"), and it moves to a new state ("in-progress").

Drawing the states and the allowed transitions forces the question: "can a completed task go back to open?" If the answer is "hmm," you've just found a business rule nobody had stated — which is precisely the point.

options: States an object can be in, and the events that move it between them
check.question: A state machine diagram shows…

screens.heading: Things that change: states
screens.keyPoint: States + events = the object's life story.

screens.body:
An operation specification describes exactly what ONE process does, step by step. Structured English is the tool: plain sentences with programming-like structure — IF this, THEN that, REPEAT until done — but no actual code.

Example: "IF payment succeeds THEN mark task completed AND notify both users; ELSE mark payment failed AND notify the poster." Anyone can read it — including the client — and a developer can turn it into code without guessing.

options: A step-by-step process description in structured plain language
check.question: An operation specification is…

screens.heading: Specifying the steps
screens.keyPoint: Precise enough to code from; plain enough for clients.

screens.body:
CASE tools — computer-aided software engineering — are apps that help you analyze and design: drawing UML diagrams, storing everything in one shared repository, and running consistency checks ("you deleted that class, but three diagrams still reference it!").

The real power isn't the drawing — it's the checking. A CASE tool is like a spellchecker for your design: it catches the inconsistencies humans gloss over, especially on team projects where five people edit the same model.

options: Software that helps draw, store, and consistency-check design models
check.question: CASE tools are…

screens.heading: Tools that check your design

screens.body:
The final validation is with the people who'll live with the system: show them the design — diagrams, prototypes, walkthroughs — and ask "does this solve your problem?" Apply usability standards to the interface parts: clear labels, forgiving errors, consistent layout.

Then integrate: interface objects and database objects join the class and sequence diagrams, so the design shows the WHOLE system — screens, logic, and data together. If it all hangs together and the client nods, you're ready to build.

options: Confirm with users/stakeholders and unify UI, logic, and data in the design
check.question: Final validation means…

screens.heading: Validate with humans
screens.keyPoint: Screens + logic + data, confirmed by real users.

screens.body: OMG (omg.org) — the official UML spec covers state machines and activity diagrams too. Nielsen Norman Group (nngroup.com) — the research behind usability standards for interface validation. IEEE (ieee.org) — standards for software reviews and verification.
screens.heading: Go deeper
screens.keyPoint: NNG wrote the book on usable interfaces.
